cards.definition_en: A number that identifies a device on a network so that other devices can send data to it.
examples: Each device on the office network receives an IP address automatically.
The log shows the IP address of every failed login.
common_mistakes: Thinking an IP address never changes for a laptop: many are assigned temporarily.
Mixing it up with a MAC address, which belongs to the network card.

cards.definition_en: A smaller part of a larger network, with its own range of addresses.
examples: The servers live in a separate subnet from the office computers.
A subnet mask shows which part of an address identifies the network.
common_mistakes: Using 'subnetwork' and 'subnet' as different things.
Thinking that devices in different subnets can never talk to each other.

cards.definition_en: A device that forwards data between different networks and decides which way each packet should go.
examples: The router connects the office network to the internet.
A misconfigured router sent traffic to the wrong place.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a modem: a modem links to the provider's line, a router directs traffic between networks.
Confusing it with a switch, which connects devices inside one network.

cards.definition_en: A device that connects computers inside one local network and passes data only to the port where the destination is.
examples: Every computer in the lab is plugged into a switch.
A managed switch lets administrators split the network into virtual parts.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a router, which links different networks.
Calling every box with many ports a switch: a hub repeats data to all ports, a switch does not.

cards.definition_en: A device or address that traffic leaves through to reach other networks, usually the router of the local network.
examples: If the default gateway is wrong, the computer cannot reach the internet.
The gateway forwards packets to the provider.
common_mistakes: Confusing a gateway with a firewall: it forwards traffic, it does not decide what is allowed.
Writing 'gate way' as two words.

cards.definition_en: The system that turns human-readable website names into the numeric addresses that computers use.
examples: The site was unreachable because the DNS record pointed to an old server.
A DNS lookup happens before the browser connects to the site.
common_mistakes: Saying 'DNS system': the S already stands for system.
Thinking that DNS carries the web page itself.

cards.definition_en: A service that automatically gives devices an IP address and other network settings when they join a network.
examples: The router acts as a DHCP server for the whole house.
A DHCP lease expires after a set time and is renewed.
common_mistakes: Entering every address by hand when DHCP is available.
Confusing DHCP with DNS: one hands out addresses, the other translates names.

cards.definition_en: A technique in which a router replaces the private addresses of internal devices with its own public address.
examples: Hundreds of students share one public address because of NAT.
Devices behind NAT cannot be reached directly from the internet.
common_mistakes: Thinking NAT is a firewall: it hides addresses but does not inspect traffic.
Pronouncing it letter by letter: it is usually said as a word.

cards.definition_en: A small unit of data sent over a network, made of a header with addressing information and a part carrying the actual data.
examples: The file was split into thousands of packets before it was sent.
The analyst captured a packet to see the request.
common_mistakes: Using 'package' for the network unit.
Thinking that all packets of one file take the same route.

cards.definition_en: An agreed set of rules that defines how two programs or devices exchange data.
examples: HTTP is the protocol that web browsers use to ask for pages.
Both ends must support the same protocol version.
common_mistakes: Confusing a protocol with the program that implements it.
Stressing the second syllable: the stress falls on the first one.

cards.definition_en: The maximum amount of data that a connection can carry in a given time.
examples: The video call stutters because the bandwidth is shared by many users.
The provider sells connections with higher bandwidth for a fee.
common_mistakes: Treating it as the same as the real speed you get: that is throughput.
Thinking more bandwidth always means lower latency.

cards.definition_en: A situation in which some packets sent over a network never arrive at their destination.
examples: Packet loss made the voice call sound broken.
The monitoring system alerts the team when packet loss exceeds one percent.
common_mistakes: Saying 'packets losing' instead of the noun phrase.
Assuming lost packets are always resent: it depends on the protocol.

cards.definition_en: Variation in the time it takes packets to arrive, which spoils real-time audio and video.
examples: High jitter makes the video call freeze and then jump forward.
A jitter buffer smooths out uneven packet arrival.
common_mistakes: Confusing jitter with latency: latency is the delay, jitter is its variation.
Spelling it 'gitter' or 'jiter'.

cards.definition_en: A component that spreads incoming requests across several servers so that none of them is overloaded.
examples: The load balancer sends each new request to the least busy server.
If a server fails its health check, the load balancer stops using it.
common_mistakes: Thinking a load balancer makes a single server faster.
Writing 'load ballancer' with a double l.

cards.definition_en: A server that makes requests on behalf of another computer, so the destination sees this server and not the original sender.
examples: Employees reach the internet through a company proxy.
The proxy hides the address of the real client.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a reverse proxy, which stands in front of servers.
Assuming a proxy always encrypts traffic.

cards.definition_en: A server placed in front of one or more web servers that receives client requests and passes them on, hiding the servers behind it.
examples: The reverse proxy terminates the encrypted connection and forwards plain requests inside the network.
Clients never talk to the application servers directly because of the reverse proxy.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with a normal proxy, which works for the client, not the server.
Thinking it is only used for caching.

cards.definition_en: A service that creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and another network, so traffic passes through it privately.
examples: Employees must turn on the VPN before opening internal tools.
A VPN protects traffic on public Wi-Fi from other users of the network.
common_mistakes: Thinking a VPN makes you completely anonymous.
Saying 'VPN network': the N already stands for network.

cards.definition_en: A numbered entry point on a computer that lets different services receive network connections separately.
examples: Web servers usually listen on port 443 for encrypted traffic.
The scan showed an unexpected open port on the server.
common_mistakes: Confusing a software port (a number) with a hardware port (a socket).
Believing that closing a port removes the program listening on it.

cards.definition_en: A protocol that delivers data reliably and in the right order by confirming that packets have arrived.
examples: Web pages are normally delivered over a TCP connection.
TCP resends packets that were not acknowledged.
common_mistakes: Thinking TCP is faster than UDP: it is more reliable, but it adds overhead.
Mixing it up with IP, which only addresses and routes packets.

cards.definition_en: A simple protocol that sends data without checking whether it arrives, which makes it fast and suitable for live audio and games.
examples: Voice calls often use UDP because a late packet is useless anyway.
DNS queries are usually sent over UDP.
common_mistakes: Expecting UDP to resend lost data.
Thinking UDP is insecure by definition; it simply gives no delivery guarantee.

cards.definition_en: The three messages that two computers exchange to set up a TCP connection before sending data.
examples: A client starts the three-way handshake by sending a SYN message.
The server did not answer, so the three-way handshake never finished.
common_mistakes: Thinking it needs three computers.
Mixing it up with the handshake of TLS, which comes after the TCP one.

cards.definition_en: A hardware identifier assigned to a network card, used to deliver data inside a local network.
examples: The switch learns the MAC address of every connected device.
MAC address filtering is easy to bypass because addresses can be changed.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the Mac computer or with an IP address.
Believing it travels across the internet: it is only used inside a local network.

cards.definition_en: A way of splitting one physical network into separate logical networks, so groups of devices cannot see each other's traffic.
examples: Guest devices are placed in a different VLAN from the staff computers.
A VLAN tag marks to which virtual network a frame belongs.
common_mistakes: Treating VLANs alone as a security boundary: if a router connects them, traffic between VLANs still needs filtering rules.
Mixing it up with a VPN, which protects traffic between distant networks.

cards.definition_en: Dividing a network into separate zones with controlled links between them, so a problem in one zone does not spread everywhere.
examples: Network segmentation kept the infection inside the guest zone.
The audit recommended better network segmentation of the payment systems.
common_mistakes: Thinking segmentation is the same as installing a single firewall.
Writing 'segmantation'.

cards.definition_en: A simple test that sends a small message to another computer and measures how long the reply takes.
examples: A high ping to the game server makes the game hard to play.
The server does not answer a ping, but the website still works.
common_mistakes: Thinking no reply to a ping means the server is down: pings may be blocked.
Using 'pinging' as a noun for the test itself.
